title: How Cognitive Biases Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore cognitive biases, the unconscious mental shortcuts (heuristics) that lead people to predictable errors in judgment. They cover the origins of the field in the work of Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, System one vs. system two thinking, and a long list of biases including hindsight bias, self-serving bias, fundamental attribution error, anchoring, decoy effect, framing, availability heuristic, inattentional blindness (the gorilla test), Dunning-Kruger effect, gambler's fallacy, base rate fallacy, mere exposure effect, illusory truth effect, and confirmation bias. The episode also covers prospect theory and behavioral economics, how biases affect medicine and forensics, tips for counteracting biases, and a listener mail correction about the origin of the name Sebastopol, California.
topics: system one and system two thinking

segments.title: Opening banter and heuristics
segments.summary: Hosts open the episode and introduce heuristics as brain shortcuts that lead to cognitive biases, with the point that biases are unconscious and affect everyone.

segments.title: Origins: Tversky and Kahneman
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck describe Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, Israeli psychologists whose partnership challenged the rational actor model and launched the Heuristics and Biases program.

segments.title: System one, system two, and the Stroop effect
segments.summary: Kahneman's fast and slow thinking model is explained, along with John Ridley Stroop's 1935 color-word interference test and post hoc rationalization.
topics: system one and system two thinking

segments.title: Hiring bias and in-group comfort
segments.summary: Using a hiring example, the hosts discuss how first impressions get rationalized afterward and how comfort with similar people entrenches organizations, which is one reason diversity programs exist.

segments.title: Why biases exist and their universality
segments.summary: The hosts note that biases arise from mental shortcuts and human guessing tendencies, and that many have been found across cultures despite replication issues and WEIRD sample criticisms.

segments.title: Hindsight, self-serving bias, and anchoring
segments.summary: Hindsight bias, self-serving bias with fundamental attribution error, and anchoring bias are explained, including the Mississippi River estimate study and the framing example of a drug mortality rate.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Availability heuristic
segments.summary: The availability heuristic is described as relying on whatever comes easily to mind, such as recent plane crash news inflating risk estimates.

segments.title: Inattentional blindness and the gorilla test
segments.summary: The hosts describe Daniel Simons' selective attention basketball test in which half of viewers miss a person in a gorilla suit, and discuss how attention is limited.

segments.title: Dunning-Kruger effect
segments.summary: The Dunning-Kruger effect is explained as overestimation by low-skill people and the reverse for experts, along with notes that the academic finding is being challenged.

segments.title: Gambler's fallacy and base rate fallacy
segments.summary: Gambler's fallacy is illustrated with blackjack and coin tosses. The base rate fallacy is illustrated with the fit woman who may be a teacher rather than a personal trainer.

segments.title: Mere exposure and illusory truth effect
segments.summary: Mere exposure effect (liking increases with familiarity) and the illusory truth effect (repeated lies become believed) are discussed, with a political aside.

segments.title: Confirmation bias, belief perseverance, and backfire effect
segments.summary: Peter Wason's 2-4-6 number sequence experiment is explained as an example of confirmation bias. The hosts discuss media bubbles, belief perseverance, the backfire effect, and why people resist challenges to their beliefs.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Second, longer break before behavioral economics.

segments.title: Behavioral economics, Thaler, and prospect theory
segments.summary: Behavioral economics is introduced as building on Tversky and Kahneman's work and Richard Thaler's predictability of biases. Prospect theory's 1979 paper, loss aversion, and the 1996 lottery ticket experiment are described, along with a 2020 replication across nineteen countries.

segments.title: Rare events and relative versus absolute thinking
segments.summary: The hosts discuss overestimating rare events, the kidnapping fear example, and relative thinking about saving money on a shirt versus a car.

segments.title: Biases in medicine and forensics
segments.summary: Biases in medical decision making, such as anchoring to first lab results and outcome bias, are discussed with reference to the show The Pit. Forensic science biases and flawed lineups are also mentioned.

segments.title: Tips for counteracting biases
segments.summary: Tips include awareness, delaying decisions, sleeping on big decisions, writing down expectations, Bayesian reasoning, a growth mindset, recognizing scarcity and social proof, and cognitive bias modification for anxiety. The hosts note AI systems may show emergent biases.

segments.title: Listener mail: Sebastopol name origin
segments.summary: Listener Marsha writes that Sebastopol, California was originally named Pine Grove and was renamed after a bar fight comparison to the Crimean War siege. The hosts also briefly discuss Iron Maiden's song about the Light Brigade.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and give the show's email and credits.
